Empirical Research Plan ‑ “Long‐Run Economic Consequences of 1930s Plains Soil Erosion”

--------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered-event-study dynamics.  
Why appropriate:  
• We observe the same counties repeatedly (balanced panel 1910-1990s).  
• Soil-erosion severity is time-invariant (permanent, measured ex post on 1940 SCS map) but its economic impact begins only once the Dust Bowl shock occurs (≈1930-40).  
• This structure permits a two-way-fixed-effects DID (county & year FEs) and an event-study that traces βτ for each census wave τ relative to 1930.  
• The treatment can be coded as either (i) discrete (High-erosion vs. Low-erosion counties) or (ii) continuous (share of original topsoil lost).  
• The pre-1930 period (1910, 1920, 1925, 1930) provides rich pre-trends tests.

Robustness/Complement:  
• Continuous-treatment “dose–response” using interacted county FEs à la Callaway-Sant’Anna or Gardner (2022).  
• IV robustness: instrument %-topsoil-loss with a wind-erosion-susceptibility index constructed from 1910 soil texture & 1895-1925 average wind velocity × drought exposure.  

--------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable:  
Treatedc = 1 if county c lost ≥50 % of original topsoil by 1940 (High erosion).  
Alt.: Continuous Ec = % topsoil lost (0–100).

Control group:  
Counties in the same 12 Plains states that lost ≤25 % (Low erosion).  
Medium-erosion counties (25–49 %) can be dropped or used for dose-response robustness.

Treatment timing:  
Postt = 1 for census years ≥1940; 0 for 1910–1930 waves.  
Event-study: τ = t – 1930 (-20,-10,0,+10,…,+60).

No running variable or cutoff is needed (not RDD).

--------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel-trends: In the absence of the erosion shock, high- and low-erosion counties would have followed parallel paths in outcomes (land values, revenues, etc.).  
Plausibility: Both groups are in the same states, share wheat monoculture boom of the 1910s, and face identical federal/state policy environments. Pre-1930 data permit direct testing.

A2. No differential contemporaneous shocks correlated with erosion after 1930 (other than erosion itself).  
Plausibility: Drought severity varied widely but can be observed (Palmer index). New Deal spending, banking failures, and AAA production controls are observable and can be controlled for.

A3. Stable treatment assignment & no anticipation: Erosion status is determined by ex-post physical loss. Farmers could not perfectly foresee which quarter-sections would lose 75 % of topsoil. Thus pre-treatment decisions should not differentially affect treated vs. control trends.

A4. SUTVA / no spatial spillovers: Outcomes in a low-erosion county are not directly affected by neighboring high-erosion counties (or effects are small). Given thousand-acre county scale, this is plausible but must be probed (e.g., border-county sample).

--------------------------------------------------
4. Primary Threats & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------
T1. Violation of parallel pre-trends (soil quality already in decline where erosion later worst).  
• Test: Estimate event-study coefficients for 1910–30 (τ = ‑20,-10).  
• Mitigate: Add county-specific linear trends; restrict sample to counties with similar 1910 soil texture & rainfall; nearest-neighbor matching on 1910 covariates.

T2. Drought-severity confounding (drier counties both eroded more and suffered larger output losses).  
• Control: Include county-year Palmer Drought Severity Index and temperature; interact with post dummy.  
• Instrument robustness: Use pre-1930 wind-erosion risk × drought to predict erosion.

T3. Policy endogeneity (New Deal conservation and relief programs disproportionately directed to high-erosion counties).  
• Control: County-year AAA payment dollars, SCS project dollars, WPA, PWA, REA spending (Fishback data).  
• Triple-diff: Compare outcomes between high and low erosion counties before and after AAA within states, interacting with annual spending intensity.  
• Interpretation: Estimate β as “net of policy response”; present bounds (Oster 2019) for potential bias.

--------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------- 0. Packages -------------
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(ggplot2); library(did); # Callaway-Sant’Anna
# ------------- 1. Load -------------
dt <- fread("plains_panel_1910_1992.csv")   # balanced panel

# ------------- 2. Variable construction -------------
# Treatment intensity
dt[, erosion_high := (topsoil_loss_pct >= 50)]
dt[, erosion_low  := (topsoil_loss_pct <= 25)]
dt <- dt[erosion_high | erosion_low]        # baseline sample
dt[, treat := as.integer(erosion_high)]

# Time – event study relative to 1930
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= 1940)]
dt[, rel_year := year - 1930]

# Factor dummies for event-study
for(tau in sort(unique(dt$rel_year))){
  dt[, paste0("D",tau) := as.integer(rel_year == tau)]
}

# Controls
ctrls <- c("palmer_z", "avg_temp", "newdeal_pc", "fdic_failures",
           "bank_susp_pc", "state_year_fe")  # state*year FE added below

# ------------- 3. Main DID -------------
feols_main <- feols(log(farmland_value_acre) ~ treat*post | county + year,
                    data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(feols_main)

# ------------- 4. Event-study -------------
event_form <- paste0("log(farmland_value_acre) ~ ",
                     paste(paste0("i(rel_year, treat, ref = -0)"), collapse = " + "),
                     " | county + year")
fe_event <- feols(as.formula(event_form), data = dt, cluster = ~state)
iplot(fe_event)  # dynamic graph

# ------------- 5. Robustness: county-specific trends -------------
fe_trends <- feols(log(farmland_value_acre) ~ treat*post + i(year, county) |
                   county + year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(fe_trends)

# ------------- 6. Robustness: C-S DID with continuous treatment -------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "log(farmland_value_acre)",
             tname = "year", gname = "first_treat_year", # =1940 for treated
             idname = "county", xformla = ~palmer_z + newdeal_pc,
             data = dt)
agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)
```

--------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)
--------------------------------------------------
• Initial (1940) drop in per-acre farmland values in high-erosion counties ≈ 30–40 % relative to low-erosion neighbors (β ≈ ‑0.35 in logs).  
• Agricultural revenue per acre falls similarly; cropland acreage converted to pasture/fallow increases 10–15 pp.  
• Over time partial recovery: by 1980 gap shrinks to ≈ 10–15 %.  
• Labor adjustment: farm population declines 5–10 % more; non-farm manufacturing employment grows modestly (+2–3 pp) as counties diversify.  
• Net present discounted loss of land rents likely remains substantial (maybe half of the initial loss persists).

--------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------
C1. Pre-trend equivalence (tested & passes?) …………… 0.8  
C2. No anticipation of treatment ……………………………… 1  
C3. Stable treatment assignment (no switching) ………… 1  
C4. No interference/spillovers ………………………………… 0.6  
C5. No time-varying confounders correlated with treatment
     after controls …………………………………………………… 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.82 → Reasonably credible but not bulletproof; main weakness is potential spatial spillovers and residual correlated shocks.

--------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
